nodes.description: OROV reaches the central nervous system, producing aseptic meningitis and meningoencephalitis and prolonging the acute phase to 2-4 weeks. In earlier outbreaks viral RNA was recovered from cerebrospinal fluid; the 2025 Panama series instead found CSF consistently negative with virus detectable in urine beyond the acute phase, so the diagnostic specimen is not settled.

evidence.snippet: it can extend up to 2-4 weeks, potentially leading to meningitis or encephalitis

nodes.description: The bite of an infected Culicoides paraensis midge inoculates OROV into the dermis. The Gn/Gc glycoproteins mediate attachment and clathrin-dependent entry into permissive cells, followed by endosomal membrane fusion and cytoplasmic release of the three ribonucleoprotein segments.

nodes.description: OROV infection of the developing fetal brain causes massive neural cell death, neuroinflammation, microglial activation and neutrophil infiltration, with neurodevelopmental disruption, microcephaly and fetal death.

evidence.reference_title: Oropouche virus causes severe congenital disease in embryonic mice.
evidence.snippet: Infected embryos present with multi-organ pathology, pneumonitis, myocarditis, steatohepatitis and severe neuropathology, including microcephaly, ventriculomegaly and neural loss.
Human OROV disease, or Oropouche fever, typically begins with a fever ranging from 100.4 to 104 °F, followed by headache, chills, malaise, myalgia and arthralgia

nodes.description: OROV infects the liver, producing necroinflammatory foci that progress to massive hepatic necrosis when the type I interferon response is lost. This hepatic injury underlies the rare severe and fatal human cases and raises circulating transaminases.

evidence.reference_title: Oropouche virus causes acute hepatitis in mice controlled by type I interferons.
evidence.snippet: In both models, OROV causes focal hepatic necrosis in mice, which progresses to massive necrosis and death when the Type I interferon receptor is antagonized.

nodes.description: The L-protein RdRp transcribes and replicates the genome in the cytoplasm using a cap-snatching mechanism, N encapsidates the segments, and the M-encoded glycoproteins assemble and bud at the Golgi. The non-structural NSs protein antagonizes the host type I interferon response, permitting early high-titre viraemia; a conserved motif at the NSs carboxy terminus is critical for this interferon-antagonistic activity.
nodes.id: OROV Genome Replication and Interferon Antagonism

biological_processes: NSs-mediated suppression of the host type I interferon response

evidence.snippet: These viral protein-RNA complexes facilitate genome replication and transcription in the cytoplasm of infected cells. Translation occurs via a cap-snatching mechanism

the viral NSs protein is an interferon (IFN) antagonist, consistent with other NSs-encoding orthobunyaviruses. We identified a conserved motif at the NSs carboxy terminus critical for this IFN antagonistic activity

nodes.description: Maternal viraemia leads to hematogenous transplacental infection of the fetoplacental unit and fetal multi-organ infection, with neurotropic damage to the developing fetal brain.

evidence.snippet: vRNA was detected in the umbilical cord blood and various foetal tissues, including the foetal brain, liver, kidneys, lungs, heart and spleen. This is now the first confirmed case of OROV vertical transmission.

evidence.reference_title: Oropouche virus infection in pregnant women in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil: a prospective cohort study.
evidence.snippet: Fetal loss and haemorrhage risk were three times higher in women with confirmed infection than in those with no infection
